fields.title: Research begins with the decision that depends on it
fields.keyTakeaway: Useful research is tied to a decision: what we are deciding, which options we are considering, and which answer will tip the choice. Research “to better understand users” leads nowhere and never ends.
fields.checkQuestion: The team asks for a “satisfaction study”. What two questions will you ask before starting?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key question of the node: **what research is needed for the company's goals?** In blocks D1 and D2, we applied individual methods; here it is about choosing between them and setting the research task.
fields.blocks/1/text: End-to-end example: Smena is a fictional shift scheduling service for small cafes and stores. The company has grown: now three people handle research, and the question of “what to study next quarter” has become real.
fields.blocks/2/text: **What happens if you do not answer this question.** Research turns into a stream of reports that no one opens. A year later, the company has a library of knowledge and not a single decision made based on it.
fields.blocks/3/subtitle: Five lines you should not start without
fields.blocks/3/items/0: **Decision** — what exactly we will decide based on the results. If the answer is “nothing, just find out”, research is not needed.
fields.blocks/3/items/1: **Options** — what we are choosing between. There must be at least two of them, otherwise the decision has already been made.
fields.blocks/3/items/2: **What will tip the choice** — which result will lean toward which option. Formulated before data collection.
fields.blocks/3/items/3: **Timeline and cost of the decision** — how much time is available and what an error will cost. An expensive and irreversible decision justifies expensive research; a cheap one does not.
fields.blocks/3/items/4: **What is already known** — past research and data. Half of all requests are closed here.
fields.blocks/4/subtitle: The method follows from the question, not vice versa
fields.blocks/4/items/0: **Why this is happening** — interviews and observation. Numbers are useless here.
fields.blocks/4/items/1: **How many people and how often** — product data, a survey on a large sample.
fields.blocks/4/items/2: **What a person will choose** — an experiment or observing behavior; asking is useless.
fields.blocks/4/items/3: **Is it clear** — a usability test with five to eight people. No more is needed: problems repeat.
fields.blocks/4/items/4: **Is it worth doing at all** — it is often cheaper to manually simulate a feature than to study intent.
fields.blocks/5/text:
Request 1: “Study user satisfaction”.
Questions: what decision depends on it? — “none, for understanding”. Rejected.

Request 2: “Understand why cafes with one location churn in the third month”.
Decision: whether to make a separate simplified tier or improve the current product.
What will tip the choice: if they leave due to price — a tier; if because a schedule for a single location is easier to keep in a notebook — a tier won't help.
Method: 8 interviews with churned users plus churn breakdown by number of locations.
Timeline: two weeks. Cost of error: a quarter of tier development.

The second study took ten days and canceled a quarter of work.
fields.blocks/6/text: If the responsible person says “we are going to do it anyway, we just want to confirm”, it is more honest not to waste time. Such studies always “confirm” — the only question is which slice of data will be picked.
fields.blocks/6/title: Research that cannot change a decision is a ritual
fields.blocks/7/text: Not everything needs to be researched. A cheap and reversible decision is easier to make and observe than to study: the cost of research must be lower than the cost of error, and this comparison is made before starting.
